questions.q: What does Replication Monitor show, per this lesson?
options: Publication/subscription status, agent state, pending command counts, and recent agent error history
Only the size of the distribution database
CPU and memory usage for the whole SQL Server instance
The T-SQL syntax used to create each publication
questions.explain: Replication Monitor is the SSMS tool for watching a topology's overall health, including agent status and pending commands.

questions.q: What is a tracer token, and what does it measure?
options: A marker transaction inserted at the publisher to measure real end-to-end latency, hop by hop, through the replication path
A security credential used to authenticate the Distribution Agent
A backup file used to restore a failed subscriber
A setting that disables replication temporarily
questions.explain: A tracer token travels from publisher log through the Log Reader Agent, distribution database, and Distribution Agent to the subscriber, with timestamps recorded at each hop.

questions.q: Why does splitting tracer token latency into publisher-to-distributor and distributor-to-subscriber matter?
options: It tells you which specific agent — Log Reader or Distribution — is the actual bottleneck, rather than just knowing replication 'feels slow'
It has no practical value beyond curiosity
It's required before replication can even start
It replaces the need for Replication Monitor entirely
questions.explain: The two-part timing isolates which agent's leg of the journey is slow, pointing directly at where to investigate.

questions.q: Why is checking agent job history often a fast first step, per this lesson?
options: Every replication agent runs as a regular SQL Server Agent job, so its history surfaces failures the same way any other Agent job would
Agent job history is the only place that shows pending command counts
Agent job history replaces the need for tracer tokens
It's not actually useful; the lesson recommends skipping it
questions.explain: Because replication agents are ordinary SQL Server Agent jobs under the hood, their job history is a familiar, quick place to check for failures.

questions.q: What does a healthy transactional replication topology typically look like, per this lesson?
options: Near-zero pending commands, consistent tracer token times, and clean agent job history with no repeated failures
A constantly growing distribution database with no agents running
Tracer tokens that never complete
Agent job history full of unexplained failures, which is considered normal
questions.explain: Healthy replication shows low latency, low pending command counts, and clean job history — deviations from that baseline are the early warning signs.
